target.title: fix(auth): prioritize explicit models.json apiKey over store profiles
target.body:
> [!NOTE]
> **AI-Assisted Contribution:** This PR was prepared and validated with the assistance of an AI coding assistant (Antigravity/Gemini).

## What Problem This Solves
Resolves a problem where the model auth subsystem ignores explicit `apiKey` (literal or SecretRef) overrides in `models.json` if store profiles exist (pr #100839).

**Symptom/Behavior:**
1. Unless `auth: "api-key"` is explicitly set (making `shouldPreferExplicitConfigApiKeyAuth` true), the literal key or SecretRef configured in `models.json` is ignored during the binding phase (falling through `providerEntryBinding` checks). The function then scans the profile store; if any profile is found for the provider, it overrides the user's explicit `apiKey` configuration.
2. Additionally, when a specific profile was requested (e.g. during failover rotation or pinned session), the early check for explicit models.json `apiKey` would bypass profile resolution entirely and return the models.json `apiKey` instead of the rotated profile, causing E2E failover tests (`rotates for overloaded assistant failures across auto-pinned profiles`) to fail.
3. In `models status` and `models auth list` commands, placeholder/marker values in the environment (e.g. `GOOGLE_API_KEY`) were treated as literal keys, causing incorrect `effective=models.json` formatting instead of falling back to store profiles.

Affected locations:
- [resolveApiKeyForProvider](file:///home/dietpi/Developer/openclaw/src/agents/model-auth.ts#L1071-L1084)
- [resolveProviderAuthOverview](file:///home/dietpi/Developer/openclaw/src/commands/models/list.auth-overview.ts#L152-L163)

## Why This Change Was Made
Implemented a surgical fix to resolve the logic discrepancy and test failures:
1. Updated `resolveApiKeyForProvider` to only check and return the configured `apiKey` (either a literal key or a resolved SecretRef) if `profileId` is NOT explicitly requested (`if (!params.profileId && !params.lockedProfile)`).
2. Refactored `isLiteral` in `src/commands/models/list.auth-overview.ts` to exclude non-secret placeholder/marker values using `!isNonSecretApiKeyMarker(...)`, and adjusted the precedence logic so that env-var markers do not override the effective auth early, allowing correct fallback to profiles/env.
3. Updated `resolveUsableCustomProviderApiKey` in `src/agents/model-auth.ts` to correctly filter out environment-resolved placeholder markers.

---

## User Impact
Corrects behavior to ensure that:
1. If a user configures `apiKey` in `models.json` under `models.providers.[provider].apiKey` as a literal API key string or a SecretRef, this configured credential takes precedence over any general auth profiles in the store, unless a specific profile is requested/rotated.
2. In user-facing CLI commands (`models status`), actual placeholder markers correctly fall back to database profiles in format outputs.

---

## Evidence

### Unit Tests / Verification Suite
We wrote three separate reproduction test files covering all scenarios of this behavior, and verified integration failover/rotation tests:
- **Reproduction Happy Path:** [repro_1_1_happy.test.ts](file:///home/dietpi/Developer/openclaw/src/agents/repro_1_1_happy.test.ts) (checks that literal `apiKey` overrides store profiles and resolves the correct label).

- **Reproduction Stress & Concurrency:** [repro_1_1_stress.test.ts](file:///home/dietpi/Developer/openclaw/src/agents/repro_1_1_stress.test.ts) (checks that concurrent resolution of multiple providers doesn't pollute state or cause race conditions).
- **E2E Rotation & Fallback Tests:** [embedded-agent-runner.run-embedded-agent.auth-profile-rotation.e2e.test.ts](file:///home/dietpi/Developer/openclaw/src/agents/embedded-agent-runner.run-embedded-agent.auth-profile-rotation.e2e.test.ts) and [model-fallback.run-embedded.e2e.test.ts](file:///home/dietpi/Developer/openclaw/src/agents/model-fallback.run-embedded.e2e.test.ts).

target.title: fix(agents): avoid false unscheduled note after shell cron add
target.body:
Closes #52972

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users who schedule reminders through a shell-driven `openclaw cron add ...` command could still receive the false note saying no reminder was scheduled in the turn.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reminder guard already trusts successful structured `cron` tool adds. This extends the same producer-side counter to successful `exec` and `bash` commands that run `openclaw cron add` and return a cron add response shaped like the CLI output.

The repair also handles the CLI warning path where `openclaw cron add --message ...` emits the missing-agent warning on stderr while still printing the successful JSON receipt on stdout. Exec aggregates stdout and stderr, so the parser now scans the aggregate for a valid cron-add JSON receipt instead of requiring the whole aggregate to be pure JSON. Failed commands and unrelated cron commands are ignored.

## User Impact

Users no longer get a contradictory unscheduled-reminder note after a shell cron add succeeds, including the default-agent warning case. Failed or unrelated shell commands still leave the guard active.

## Evidence

Redacted behavior proof, run from the PR checkout after rebasing on current `main`:

```text
command=openclaw cron add --at +1h --message <redacted> --name reminder
aggregateContainsWarning=true
aggregateContainsJsonReceipt=true
successfulCronAdds=1
hasReminderCommitment=true
falseNotePresent=false
deliveredReply=I'll remind you in an hour.
```

target.title: fix(chat): keep proof decision out of actor closure
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Swift 6.2 strict concurrency rejects `OpenClawChatSQLiteTranscriptCache.cancelCommand` because the closure passed to `CanonicalMessageProofHub.withProofDecision` captures actor-isolated SQLite state and actor methods. The failing diagnostic is `sending 'db' risks causing data races`, and it blocks `GatewayEndpointStoreTests`, the `OpenClaw` product build, and packaged app verification from current `main`.

The fix keeps the same final cancellation synchronization semantics, but replaces the closure helper with explicit `lockProofDecision` / `unlockProofDecision` calls. That keeps the final proof decision, SQLite commit, and cache removal inside the same synchronized region while leaving actor-isolated work in the actor method body.

## Summary

- replace the closure-based proof-decision helper with explicit lock/unlock calls
- preserve lock coverage around proof decision, SQLite commit, and cache cleanup
- avoid passing actor-isolated SQLite state through a synchronous nonisolated closure under Swift 6.2

## Evidence

target.title: Add reset family carryover summaries
target.body:
## Behavior or issue addressed

Depends on #90239.

When a session has been reset/rotated, the active transcript can be clean while the previous reset archive still contains the latest compaction summary. The next embedded-agent prompt therefore starts without the carryover context unless the model/tool explicitly asks for family history.

This change reuses the session-family transcript resolver from #90239 and injects the latest reset-archive compaction summary into embedded-agent prompt context before the LLM boundary, but only when the active context does not already contain a compaction summary.

## Fix

- Move the #90239 family/reset transcript target resolver into a shared gateway helper.
- Keep `chat.history(includeFamily)` on the shared resolver.
- Pass the current session store path/entry into embedded-agent attempts.
- Add a prompt-context transform that prepends one `compactionSummary` from reset ancestor transcripts.
- Skip injection when the active session already has a compaction summary.
- Cap family transcript read targets before reading files; ancestor targets stop at the cap while current-session targets remain available.
- Rebased onto current `origin/main` and preserved the newer transcript-reader seam plus same-session reset fallback.

## Real behavior proof

**Current head proven:** `ba74ecd54e52c2416ab8f7906491266b989f529c`.

**Behavior or issue addressed:** A reset/rotated logical session should read bounded reset-family history through the shared resolver, keep current reset archive plus current active transcript available inside the cap, preserve the newest eligible ancestors even when an older retained ancestor has many reset-topic archives, and inject exactly one reset-family compaction summary before the embedded-agent LLM boundary.

Closes #101770

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `openclaw cron edit --failure-alert-cooldown 0.1ms` could save a `0ms` failure-alert cooldown even though the user entered a positive-looking duration.

## Why This Change Was Made

The cron edit path now rejects parsed cooldown values that are falsy, matching the duration parser's invalid result for tiny durations that floor to `0ms`.

## User Impact

Users configuring cron failure alerts get a clear validation error instead of accidentally disabling cooldown throttling.

target.title: fix: require exact markdown frontmatter fences
target.body:
Closes #101769

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Markdown that starts with dash-prefixed text such as `---not` or `----` could be treated as a frontmatter block.

## Why This Change Was Made

Frontmatter parsing, bundled command body stripping, and skill workshop proposal stripping now require opening and closing fences to be whole `---` lines. This keeps ordinary dash-prefixed Markdown content from being parsed or stripped as metadata.

## User Impact

Plugin command, hook, skill, metadata, and workshop proposal Markdown that begins with non-delimiter dash text is preserved as body content instead of being misread as frontmatter.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(agents): resolve fable-5 1M context window for claude-cli provider
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`claude-cli + claude-fable-5` falls back to the default 200K context window instead of 1M. The `resolveAnthropicFixedContextWindow` Fable 5 guard only matched `anthropic` and `anthropic-vertex` providers, leaving `claude-cli` unhandled.

Both call paths were affected:
- `resolveContextTokensForModelFromCache` (direct context resolution)
- `resolveDiscoveredAnthropicFixedContextWindow` (discovery cache upgrade)

Same root cause as #100572: a new model was added to the catalog but the `claude-cli` provider boundary was not enumerated in the Fable 5 guard.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add `provider === 'claude-cli'` to the existing Fable 5 fixed-window guard, matching the pattern already used by the Mythos 5 / Sonnet 5 guards and the GA 1M prefix check on the next branch.

## User Impact

`claude-cli/claude-fable-5` now correctly resolves to 1,000,000 token context window via `ANTHROPIC_FABLE_CONTEXT_TOKENS`. All three Anthropic-affiliated providers (anthropic, anthropic-vertex, claude-cli) now receive the correct fixed context window for Fable 5.

target.title: fix(security): bound mcporter registry read in audit
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readGlobalMcporterRegistrySummary` in `src/security/audit.ts` read the global MCP registry (`stateDir/skills/config/mcporter.json`) with an unbounded `fs.readFile`, so a maliciously large or corrupted registry could exhaust memory during a security audit.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replaced the unbounded read with `readRegularFile`, which rejects symlinks and non-files and supports a byte cap. A 16 MiB limit is consistent with other bounded config reads in the codebase. If the file exceeds the limit or cannot be read, the function returns `null`, treating the oversized registry the same as a missing one.

## User Impact

Security audit no longer buffers an unbounded registry file into memory; behavior is unchanged for normal-sized registries.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test that writes a `16 MiB + 1` byte `mcporter.json` and asserts the `tools.exec.agent_skill_mcp_boundary_drift` finding is not emitted.

target.title: fix(session-memory): bound session transcript reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`getRecentSessionContent` in `src/hooks/bundled/session-memory/transcript.ts` reads session transcript JSONL files with an unbounded `fs.promises.readFile` call. A runaway or corrupted session file could force the session-memory extraction path to buffer the entire file into memory, leading to OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

Session-memory extraction now uses a bounded hybrid reader:
- For transcripts that fit under the 16 MiB cap, it streams lines newest-first through the shared `streamSessionTranscriptLinesReverse` helper and stops before retaining a line that would cross the cap.
- For transcripts that exceed the cap, it reads only the trailing 16 MiB and drops the first partial JSONL line, so a single over-cap record is not materialized.

This avoids whole-file buffering while preserving recent session context.

## User Impact

Session-memory extraction now safely bounds oversized transcripts while still keeping the most recent messages available for context.

## Evidence

- Added regression tests covering:
  - a transcript exceeding the cap with recent trailing messages — asserts the recent messages are preserved and the huge early message is absent,
  - a single JSONL row larger than the cap — asserts `getRecentSessionContent` returns `null`.
- Local focused run: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/hooks/bundled/session-memory/transcript.test.ts --run` passes (5/5 tests).

## Real behavior proof (standalone)

I ran a standalone Node script outside Vitest that imports the actual changed helper from source and exercises both the oversized-tail path and the lone over-cap row path.

Script: `/tmp/proof-101475.mjs` (not committed).

```text
$ node --import tsx /tmp/proof-101475.mjs
=== Case 1: oversized transcript with recent tail ===
File size: 17826089 bytes (cap is 16777216 bytes)
Result contains recent user message: true
Result contains recent assistant message: true
Result does NOT contain huge early message: true
Result length under cap: true

=== Case 2: lone over-cap JSONL row ===
Result is null: true
```

The helper bounds reads for both pathological layouts without buffering the entire transcript into memory.

target.title: improve(google): identify OpenClaw Gemini API traffic

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw should be identifiable when it calls the Gemini API on a user's behalf. Today, those API-key requests do not include Google's documented partner/library attribution header, so Gemini traffic from OpenClaw is harder to distinguish from other client traffic.

AI-assisted: yes, implemented with Codex and reviewed locally.

## Why This Change Was Made

Google's Gemini API partner integration guidance asks partner and library integrations to send `x-goog-api-client` with a product/version token. This change adds `x-goog-api-client: openclaw/<version>` across OpenClaw's Gemini API paths, including direct REST calls, shared provider request policy, the GenAI SDK wrapper, embeddings, web search, video fallback, streaming, and prompt cache calls.

Authentication is intentionally unchanged. API-key calls still use `x-goog-api-key`, OAuth-style calls still use `Authorization: Bearer`, and the new attribution header is added alongside the existing auth headers.

## User Impact

Users do not need to change any settings. Operators and maintainers can expect Gemini API traffic from OpenClaw to carry OpenClaw attribution in the way Google asks partner integrations to identify themselves.

target.title: add per-conversation whatsapp debounce config
target.body:
## Summary

Adds per-conversation inbound debounce configuration for WhatsApp direct chats and groups.

Practically, this controls how long OpenClaw waits before starting an agent turn after receiving a WhatsApp message from a specific conversation. This is useful when a contact sends multiple messages in a row: OpenClaw can wait a few seconds or minutes, collect the full burst, and then let the agent process the conversation with better context.

## What Problem This Solves

The existing WhatsApp debounce setting is too broad for mixed usage.

Some conversations should be processed immediately, while others should wait briefly:

- owner/admin chats often need immediate processing, so they can use `debounceMs: 0`
- external contacts often send multiple short messages in a row, so they can use a longer debounce, such as `180000`, to wait 3 minutes
- noisy groups can have their own debounce window
- wildcard entries can define defaults for all direct chats or all groups

This lets operators tune batching by conversation without changing the global WhatsApp debounce for every chat.

## Behavior

- supports `debounceMs` in `channels.whatsapp.direct`
- supports `debounceMs` in `channels.whatsapp.groups`
- supports wildcard entries like `direct["*"]` and `groups["*"]`
- specific conversation config wins over wildcard config
- falls back to the existing global WhatsApp debounce when no conversation override exists
- `debounceMs: 0` disables debounce for that conversation only

## Evidence

Redacted real WhatsApp setup proof from a local OpenClaw home:

The run used the PR branch plus real WhatsApp session keys from the local OpenClaw session index. The proof output prints only counts and redacted aliases; it does not include phone numbers, group JIDs, contact names, credentials, or message bodies. It feeds those real direct/group session keys through the same keyed inbound debouncer that the WhatsApp listener calls through `resolveDebounceMs`.

```text
$ node --import tsx <redacted local proof script>
   0ms real-session-inventory direct=200 group=3
   0ms config <redacted-direct-1> debounceMs=0
   0ms config <redacted-direct-2> debounceMs=120
   0ms config <redacted-group-1> debounceMs=180
   0ms flush <redacted-direct-1> items=1 debounceMs=0
   0ms flush <redacted-direct-1> items=1 debounceMs=0
 151ms flush <redacted-direct-2> items=2 debounceMs=120
 220ms flush <redacted-group-1> items=2 debounceMs=180
# exit code 0
```

This shows the changed batching behavior with real WhatsApp conversation identifiers redacted: the `debounceMs: 0` direct override flushes two messages immediately as separate items, while the other direct conversation and the group conversation batch two quick messages into one flush using their own per-conversation windows.

target.title: fix(matrix): tolerate SAS accept events missing method
target.body:
Closes #96188

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Matrix users could get stuck during SAS verification when Element sends an encrypted `m.key.verification.accept` to-device event without a `method` field. In that shape, matrix-js-sdk's Rust crypto preprocessing rejects the event before the Matrix plugin can continue the verification flow.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Matrix client now installs a narrow compatibility wrapper after `initRustCrypto()` that normalizes only `m.key.verification.accept` to-device events with missing or blank `content.method` to the SAS method (`m.sas.v1`) before Rust crypto preprocesses them. Existing methods, unrelated events, and the original event objects are left untouched.

This is intentionally scoped to the matrix-js-sdk Rust crypto preprocessor boundary because `/sync` to-device events reach Rust crypto before higher-level JS `MatrixEvent` compatibility hooks can run.

## User Impact

Matrix SAS verification with Element can continue instead of stalling on an opaque missing-field crypto error. There are no config, setup, or API changes.

## Evidence

- Rechecked live issue state: #96188 is open, and `gh pr list --repo openclaw/openclaw --state open --search "96188"` returned no superseding open PRs.
- Checked dependency behavior in local `matrix-js-sdk` source: `/sync` to-device events are sent through `cryptoCallbacks.preprocessToDeviceMessages()`, and the Rust crypto backend calls `receiveSyncChanges()` before JS compatibility events are emitted.
- Checked the current Matrix client-server spec for `m.key.verification.accept`; the SAS accept example carries `method: "m.sas.v1"`.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/matrix/src/matrix/sdk/to-device-compat.test.ts extensions/matrix/src/matrix/sdk/crypto-facade.test.ts extensions/matrix/src/matrix/sdk/verification-manager.test.ts`

target.title: fix(security): bound plugin manifest reads in audit deep scan
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readPluginManifestExtensions` in `src/security/audit-extra.async.ts` read each installed plugin's `package.json` with an unbounded `fs.readFile`. A malicious or broken plugin could place an arbitrarily large manifest in the plugin directory and exhaust memory or slow the security audit.

## Why This Change Was Made

The audit deep scan now enforces a hard 1 MiB size limit on plugin `package.json` reads, using the existing `statRegularFile` / `readRegularFile` helpers from `src/infra/regular-file.js`, which also reject symlinks and non-file targets. Oversized manifests throw a clear error that surfaces as a `plugins.code_safety.manifest_parse_error` finding, matching the existing malformed-JSON behavior so the issue is visible instead of silently skipped.

## User Impact

Users will receive a clear security audit warning if any installed plugin manifest exceeds 1 MiB, and the audit will no longer attempt to load unbounded file content during deep scan.

## Evidence

target.title: fix: handle Telegram reaction count updates
target.body:
## Summary
- request Telegram `message_reaction_count` updates alongside `message_reaction`
- add a dedicated `message_reaction_count` handler that emits aggregate reaction-count system events for allowed groups
- route reaction-count updates through the Telegram sequential key and document the actorless aggregate-count semantics

## Why
PR #93731 was closed because it subscribed to `message_reaction_count` updates without a runtime handler. That would let polling/webhook accept count updates and then silently drop them. This patch pairs the subscription with explicit aggregate-count handling, routing, docs, and tests.

## Behavior
- `message_reaction` still handles per-user reaction additions.
- `message_reaction_count` now emits events like `Telegram reaction counts changed: 👍 x3, 🔥 x2 on msg 42`.
- Aggregate count updates have no actor identity, so OpenClaw treats them as chat-level group events. Private chats are skipped, and sender-only allowlists do not authorize anonymous aggregate counts.
- Forum group count updates route to the general-topic session, matching existing reaction routing where Telegram omits thread IDs.

## Tests
- `./node_modules/.bin/vitest run extensions/telegram/src/allowed-updates.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/sequential-key.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/bot.test.ts`
- `./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check extensions/telegram/src/bot-handlers.runtime.ts extensions/telegram/src/bot.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/sequential-key.ts extensions/telegram/src/sequential-key.test.ts`

target.title: fix(auth): prioritize explicit models.json apiKey over store profiles
target.body:
> [!NOTE]
> **AI-Assisted Contribution:** This PR was prepared and validated with the assistance of an AI coding assistant (Antigravity/Gemini).

## What Problem This Solves
Resolves a problem where the model auth subsystem ignores explicit `apiKey` (literal or SecretRef) overrides in `models.json` if store profiles exist (pr #100839).

**Symptom/Behavior:**
1. Unless `auth: "api-key"` is explicitly set (making `shouldPreferExplicitConfigApiKeyAuth` true), the literal key or SecretRef configured in `models.json` is ignored during the binding phase (falling through `providerEntryBinding` checks). The function then scans the profile store; if any profile is found for the provider, it overrides the user's explicit `apiKey` configuration.
2. Additionally, when a specific profile was requested (e.g. during failover rotation or pinned session), the early check for explicit models.json `apiKey` would bypass profile resolution entirely and return the models.json `apiKey` instead of the rotated profile, causing E2E failover tests (`rotates for overloaded assistant failures across auto-pinned profiles`) to fail.
3. In `models status` and `models auth list` commands, placeholder/marker values in the environment (e.g. `GOOGLE_API_KEY`) were treated as literal keys, causing incorrect `effective=models.json` formatting instead of falling back to store profiles.

Affected locations:
- [resolveApiKeyForProvider](file:///home/dietpi/Developer/openclaw/src/agents/model-auth.ts#L1071-L1084)
- [resolveProviderAuthOverview](file:///home/dietpi/Developer/openclaw/src/commands/models/list.auth-overview.ts#L152-L163)

## Why This Change Was Made
Implemented a surgical fix to resolve the logic discrepancy and test failures:
1. Updated `resolveApiKeyForProvider` to only check and return the configured `apiKey` (either a literal key or a resolved SecretRef) if `profileId` is NOT explicitly requested (`if (!params.profileId && !params.lockedProfile)`).
2. Refactored `isLiteral` in `src/commands/models/list.auth-overview.ts` to exclude non-secret placeholder/marker values using `!isNonSecretApiKeyMarker(...)`, and adjusted the precedence logic so that env-var markers do not override the effective auth early, allowing correct fallback to profiles/env.
3. Updated `resolveUsableCustomProviderApiKey` in `src/agents/model-auth.ts` to correctly filter out environment-resolved placeholder markers.

---

## User Impact
Corrects behavior to ensure that:
1. If a user configures `apiKey` in `models.json` under `models.providers.[provider].apiKey` as a literal API key string or a SecretRef, this configured credential takes precedence over any general auth profiles in the store, unless a specific profile is requested/rotated.
2. In user-facing CLI commands (`models status`), actual placeholder markers correctly fall back to database profiles in format outputs.

---

target.title: fix(exec-approval): distinguish non-persistable command from ask=always policy in approval prompt
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When \`allowAlwaysPersistence.kind === "one-shot"\` (for example, a command that uses shell redirection), \`allow-always\` is correctly excluded from the allowed decisions. The approval prompt still showed the same explanation used for an \`ask=always\` policy:

> "The effective approval policy requires approval every time, so Allow Always is unavailable."

That is misleading because the command can be approved; it just cannot be saved as a reusable approval pattern.

Closes #97069

## What Changed

1. **`exec-approval-reply.ts`** — added optional `nonPersistableCommand` field to `ExecApprovalPendingReplyParams`. When true, `buildExecApprovalPendingReplyPayload` emits a distinct message explaining the command cannot be saved as a reusable pattern.

2. **`bash-tools.exec-runtime.ts`** — same branch added to `buildApprovalPendingMessage` (the foreground/CLI approval message path).

3. **`bash-tools.exec-types.ts`** — added `nonPersistableCommand?: boolean` to the `approval-pending` variant of `ExecToolDetails`, so the flag survives the gateway→tool-result→embedded-handler hop.

4. **`bash-tools.exec-host-shared.ts`** — `buildExecApprovalPendingToolResult` accepts and passes `nonPersistableCommand` through to both the message builder and the details output.

5. **`bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.ts`** — derives and passes `nonPersistableCommand: effectiveAllowAlwaysPersistence.kind === "one-shot" && hostAsk !== "always"` to the tool-result builder.

6. **`bash-tools.exec-host-node.ts`** — same derivation using `allowAlwaysPersistence` and `approvalDecisionAsk`.

7. **`embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.tools.ts`** — reads `nonPersistableCommand` from the pending details and forwards it to `buildExecApprovalPendingReplyPayload`.

8. **`exec-approval-forwarding.ts` (Telegram)** — derives `nonPersistableCommand` from `allowedDecisions` and `request.request.ask` and passes it through.

## Real Behavior Proof

**Unit tests — 188 passing across 5 test files:**

```
$ pnpm exec vitest run src/infra/exec-approval-reply.test.ts \
    src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-shared.test.ts \
    src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.test.ts

 Test Files  5 passed (5)
      Tests  188 passed (188)
   Duration  ~14s
```

**Specific non-persistable vs. policy tests in `exec-approval-reply.test.ts` (34/34):**
- `shows non-persistable message when allow-always is excluded by command type` — asserts message contains `"cannot be saved as a reusable pattern"`, not `"policy requires approval every time"`
- `shows policy message when allow-always is excluded by ask=always policy` — asserts message contains `"policy requires approval every time"`, not `"cannot be saved as a reusable pattern"`

|---|---|---|
| Gateway foreground (`buildApprovalPendingMessage`) | always policy copy | ✅ correct copy |
| Gateway tool result details (`ExecToolDetails`) | no flag | ✅ flag stored |
| Embedded handler → reply payload | no flag | ✅ flag forwarded |
| Telegram forwarder → reply payload | no flag | ✅ flag derived + forwarded |
| Node foreground | always policy copy | ✅ correct copy |

target.title: fix(tool-search): normalize flattened target-tool args for tool_call
target.body:
Fixes #96115

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where local models (e.g., vLLM/Qwen) with `agents.defaults.experimental.localModelLean: true` drop target-tool arguments when calling `tool_call` through the compact Tool Search surface. The models emit target-tool parameters (such as `command`, `path`, `task`) flattened at the top level of `tool_call` alongside `id`, rather than nesting them under `args`. This causes the target tool to receive `{}` empty arguments and repeatedly fail with `missing required parameter` errors, creating a sticky failure loop.

## Why This Change Was Made

`readCallArgs` (`src/agents/tool-search.ts:1680`) only checked `params.args` and `params.input`, returning `{}` when neither was present. Local models are less precise at schema compliance than GPT/Claude and tend to place target-tool arguments at the top level next to `id`. The fix adds a flattened fallback without breaking the existing `args` nesting contract: when both `args` and `input` are absent, collect every top-level key except `id` from `params` and pass it as the target tool's `input`.

## User Impact

Users running local models with `localModelLean: true` can now invoke tools correctly without losing arguments. Users who explicitly nest arguments under `args` are unaffected.

## Evidence

**Environment**: Linux, Node v22.23.0, pnpm v11.2.2, worktree SHA 2af06042c2


## What Problem This Solves

Agents in the web chat can only answer in text and markdown. For content that is inherently visual — flow diagrams, small dashboards, comparisons, interactive explainers — a rendered inline widget communicates far better, and OpenClaw already ships the rendering substrate (the Canvas plugin's sandboxed embed pipeline). What was missing is a first-class tool for "render this markup inline in the chat transcript," and the underlying capability such a tool needs: a way to offer a tool only where the user's client can actually render its output. Today every gateway client (web UI, iOS, Android, macOS, CLI) collapses to the same internal message channel at tool-assembly time, so a web-only tool would have appeared — and dead-ended — on phones and terminals too.

## Why This Change Was Made

Two parts, deliberately layered:

**Client-capability-gated tool availability (generic core seam).** Gateway clients already declare capability flags at connect (`GATEWAY_CLIENT_CAPS`, previously only `tool-events`). This adds an `inline-widgets` capability that the browser Control UI declares, stamps the connected client's caps into the per-run message context at `chat.send` dispatch (mirroring `GatewayClientScopes`), and threads them through the run/queue/compaction paths into tool assembly. Tools — core or plugin — can declare `requiredClientCaps`; `createOpenClawTools` drops any tool whose required caps the originating client did not declare. Channel runs (Telegram, WhatsApp, …) have no gateway client and therefore no caps, so gated tools are simply absent there, and `tools.allow` cannot resurrect them (capability is a hard availability fact, not policy). Queue collect-mode batching keys on caps so runs from different surfaces don't merge. Additive protocol only: one new capability string, no version bump, no new config keys.

**`show_widget` tool (Canvas plugin).** The agent passes a `title` plus `widget_code` (`<svg …>` or an HTML fragment, ≤256 KiB). The plugin wraps it in a minimal HTML shell and persists it through the existing Canvas document store — bounded to 32 documents per session scope, oldest evicted — and returns the canvas preview handle the web chat already knows how to render, so the widget appears inline from the tool call itself and survives history reload with zero new UI rendering machinery.

**Security model** (hardened through two structured-review cycles):
- Widget iframes never get `allow-same-origin`: the preview carries a sandbox ceiling that caps the operator's global `embedSandbox` mode, enforced on both the inline preview and the sidebar open path.
- The Canvas host serves widget documents with a `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox allow-scripts` response header, so navigating to the hosted URL directly also runs the widget in an opaque origin rather than the Control UI origin.
- The widget document's own CSP (`default-src 'none'`; inline style/script; `data:` images) blocks external fetches and resource loads; the Control UI page CSP (`default-src 'self'`, no `frame-src`) additionally restricts where embedded frames can navigate. Scripts remain allowed by design — widgets are interactive — with the residual self-navigation limitation documented on the docs page.

## User Impact

Agents talking to the web Control UI gain a `show_widget` tool and can answer with rendered, optionally interactive, self-contained widgets inline in the chat. Users on Telegram, WhatsApp, the CLI, or the native apps see no change: the tool does not exist for those runs, so agents cannot call it into a void. Plugin authors get a documented, generic way to ship surface-conditional tools (`requiredClientCaps`), and native apps can adopt the widget surface later by declaring the capability. No configuration changes are required; the existing `gateway.controlUi.embedSandbox` tiers keep applying, with widgets capped below `trusted`.

## Evidence

- Capability gating: `src/agents/openclaw-tools.client-caps.test.ts` (absent caps exclude, superset includes, channel runs exclude, `tools.allow` cannot resurrect), `src/auto-reply/reply/queue/drain.client-caps.test.ts` (collect-mode batching keys on caps), `src/gateway/server-methods/chat.directive-tags.test.ts` (ctx stamping; 270 tests), `src/plugins/tool-descriptor-cache.test.ts` (caps survive descriptor caching).
- Widget tool: `extensions/canvas/src/widget-tool.test.ts` (validation, SVG/HTML wrapping with CSP meta, opaque ids, per-scope eviction, manifest sandbox marker), `extensions/canvas/src/host/server.test.ts` (sandbox-marked documents get the CSP sandbox header and skip live reload; unmarked documents unchanged).
- Web UI: `ui/src/api/gateway.node.test.ts` (Control UI declares `inline-widgets`), `ui/src/lib/chat/tool-display.node.test.ts` (sandbox ceiling math), `ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-tool-cards.node.test.ts` (canvas handle extraction incl. sandbox; sidebar conversion preserves the ceiling), `ui/src/lib/chat/message-normalizer.test.ts`.
- `pnpm build` green with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]`; docs map/MDX/link checks green; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files; `git diff --check` clean.
- Structured autoreview ran until clean: two P1 findings surfaced and were fixed with regression tests (sidebar path dropping the sandbox ceiling under `trusted` mode; hosted widget documents executing as the app origin when opened directly), final review reported no actionable findings.
- Focused proof ran locally (hosted CI verifies the full gates at the exact head); remote box warmups were queued at the time, noted per validation policy.

target.title: fix(anthropic): add claude-fable-5 to CLI allowlist, aliases, labels, and context window
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`claude-fable-5` — a production Anthropic model — was missing from the CLI provider path (`extensions/anthropic/cli-constants.ts` + `cli-catalog.ts` + `openclaw.plugin.json`), while the direct Anthropic provider path (`register.runtime.ts`) already has full support via `isAnthropicFable5Model()` / `resolveAnthropicFixedContextWindow()`.

Five metadata layers were missing, plus the `fable`/`fable-5` aliases weren't routed through the context/model-ref canonicalization paths:

| Layer | File | Consequence |
|-------|------|-------------|
| allowlist | `cli-constants.ts` | `openclaw configure` cannot select fable-5 |
| aliases | `cli-constants.ts` | `fable` / `fable-5` aliases unresolvable |
| static manifest | `openclaw.plugin.json` | `openclaw models list` hides fable-5 |
| label | `cli-catalog.ts` | Falls back to bare `${id} (Claude CLI)` |
| context window | `cli-catalog.ts` | Falls back to 200K instead of 1M |
| context/model-ref canonicalization | `claude-model-refs.ts`, `prepare.ts` | Bare `fable` alias uses 200K fallback instead of 1M |
| **fixed context window resolver** | `context-resolution.ts` | `claude-cli` excluded from Fable 5/Mythos 5 provider checks |

This is the same root cause as #100572: a new model was registered in the direct API path but the CLI path's independently-maintained constants were not updated.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add fable-5 entries to all CLI metadata layers **and** route the `fable` family alias through both canonicalization paths:

1. `cli-constants.ts`: add `claude-cli/claude-fable-5` to allowlist, add `fable`/`fable-5`/`claude-fable-5` aliases
2. `cli-catalog.ts`: add 1M context window, friendly label, and large-image tier for fable-5
3. `openclaw.plugin.json`: add `claude-fable-5` to the static `claude-cli` provider manifest so `openclaw models list --all` shows the model
4. `claude-model-refs.ts`: add `fable: "claude-fable-5"` to `DEFAULT_CLAUDE_MODEL_BY_FAMILY` so `resolveClaudeCliAnthropicModelRefs("claude-cli/fable")` returns the correct 1M reference
5. `prepare.ts`: add `fable`/`fable-5` aliases to `CLAUDE_CLI_CONTEXT_MODEL_ALIASES` so context budgeting doesn't fall to the 200K default
6. `context-resolution.ts`: add `claude-cli` to the Fable 5 and Mythos 5 fixed context window provider checks
7. `cli-migration.test.ts`: update 3 migration test expectations to include `sonnet-5`/`fable-5` entries produced by the updated allowlist

## User Impact

- `openclaw configure` can now select `claude-fable-5` for the Claude CLI provider
- `openclaw models list --all --provider claude-cli` now shows `claude-cli/claude-fable-5` with correct 1M context
- Aliases `fable` / `fable-5` / `claude-fable-5` resolve with correct 1M context window (was 200K)

## Evidence

### Tests

- `pnpm test src/agents/context.test.ts` — 67 passed (includes `claude-cli/claude-fable-5` and `claude-cli/claude-mythos-5` context-window test cases)
- `pnpm test extensions/anthropic/cli-migration.test.ts extensions/anthropic/index.test.ts` — 52 passed (8 test files total, 119 tests across 3 suites)
- oxlint — clean
- `pnpm format:check` — clean
- CI: all passing (Critical Quality, Security High, dependency-guard, Socket Security, CodeQL, QA Smoke)

### Real Behavior Proof

Built from head `1d26a88` on Node v24.13.1 (Linux x86_64) with `pnpm build`, then verified at both module boundary and CLI level:

#### 1. CLI Model Catalog (end-to-end)

`claude-cli/claude-fable-5` appears in the full CLI catalog with 1M context window and text+image input:

```
$ pnpm openclaw models list --all --provider claude-cli

Model                                      Input      Ctx         Local Auth  Tags
claude-cli/claude-fable-5                  text+image 1000k       no    no
claude-cli/claude-opus-4-6                 text+image 200k        no    no
claude-cli/claude-opus-4-7                 text+image 200k        no    no
claude-cli/claude-opus-4-8                 text+image 1049k       no    no
claude-cli/claude-sonnet-4-6               text+image 200k        no    no    configured,alias:sonnet
claude-cli/claude-sonnet-5                 text+image 1000k       no    no
```

#### 2. JSON Catalog Entry

`claude-cli/claude-fable-5` catalog entry confirms correct metadata:

```
Key:          claude-cli/claude-fable-5
Name:         Claude Fable 5 (Claude CLI)
Input:        text+image
Context:      1,000,000
```

#### 3. Module-level Verification

```
CLI Allowlist:         claude-cli/claude-fable-5 in CLAUDE_CLI_DEFAULT_ALLOWLIST_REFS → PASS
CLI Aliases:           fable→fable, fable-5→claude-fable-5, claude-fable-5→claude-fable-5 → PASS
Catalog Entry:         id="claude-fable-5", ctx=1000000, image=maxSidePx:2576 → PASS
Context Resolution:    claude-cli/claude-fable-5 → 1000000 (was undefined before fix) → PASS
                       claude-cli/claude-mythos-5 → 1000000 (was undefined before fix) → PASS
Model Ref Resolution:  fable → rewriteRef="anthropic/claude-fable-5" → PASS
                       fable-5 → rewriteRef="anthropic/claude-fable-5" → PASS
Negative cases:        openai/claude-fable-5 → undefined ✓, google/claude-fable-5 → undefined ✓
```

#### 4. Build Verification

`pnpm build` — all phases green. All 6 Claude CLI models enumerated in built dist catalog.

### Limitations

- **Not tested with a real Claude CLI subscription.** This system does not have an active Claude subscription, so the actual `claude auth login` flow and end-to-end CLI agent turn with `claude-cli/claude-fable-5` were not exercised. The fix is source-reproducible and module-level + CLI catalog contracts are verified. A maintainer with an active Claude subscription can verify the full `openclaw configure` → select `claude-cli` → choose `claude-fable-5` flow.
- The overlapping PR #101368 (narrower context-window-only fix) should be closed or retargeted if this broader PR lands.

target.title: Dashboard: inter-widget pub/sub — a tab-scoped, parent-brokered message bus
target.body:
> Widgets on the same tab can finally talk to each other — a filter widget drives a chart, a selector narrows a table — without ever being able to reach a widget on another tab.

Closes #101147. **Stacked on #101098** — targets `main` with a cumulative diff; review `bus.ts` + the `bridge.ts` / host changes as the delta.

## What's in this PR
- Bridge messages `dashboard:publish` / `dashboard:subscribe` / `dashboard:unsubscribe` (inbound) delivering as `dashboard:message` (outbound), gated behind a new `bus:pubsub` manifest capability.
- A parent-brokered, DOM-free bus (`ui/src/lib/dashboard/bus.ts`): widgets never talk directly — the trusted parent fans a published payload out to the *other* same-tab subscribers on that channel.
- Caps: 8 KB payload, 60 publishes / 60 s (keyed by stable widget name so a remount can't reset the budget), 256-char channel names.

## Security model (this is the point of the design)
- **Tab isolation is structural, not a filter.** The subscription table is keyed `tabSlug → channel → subscriberId`, and a publish only ever iterates the *publisher's own tab bucket*. A widget on tab A cannot observe — or even enumerate — a subscriber on tab B; cross-tab delivery is unreachable code, not a rejected case.
- **Identity is broker-assigned.** The host mints an opaque `subscriberId` the widget never sees, and binds `tabSlug` from the widget's real tab (`tab.slug` in `renderGrid`) — both are closed over in the parent; a child message only ever carries an opaque `channel` + `payload`. A widget can't spoof another's identity, target a specific peer, or name a tab it wasn't assigned to. The publisher is excluded from its own broadcast.
- **No new reach.** The bus is in-memory and parent-brokered only — it never touches the gateway and never persists. The capability gate, size cap, and rate limit sit alongside the existing `sendPrompt` gates in `bridge.ts`; the `event.source` window-identity filter still guards the new inbound types; opaque origin unchanged.

All of the above is covered by tests (same-tab delivery, cross-tab non-delivery, publisher exclusion, capability denial both directions, size/rate caps, unmount teardown, unexpected-window rejection). No new dependency.

## Real behavior proof
**Behavior or issue addressed:** Dashboard widgets were fully isolated, so they couldn't compose — a filter widget had no way to drive a chart on the same tab. This adds a parent-brokered, tab-scoped pub/sub bus, capability-gated and rate/size-capped, with cross-tab isolation guaranteed by construction.
**Evidence:** `pnpm -C ui vitest run src/lib/dashboard src/components` green including the bus/bridge/host suites (tab-isolation, publisher-exclusion, capability gate, caps, unmount sweep); `pnpm ui:i18n:check`, `pnpm ui:build`, and full type-aware oxlint clean. Counts confirmed by the submitting orchestrator's own gate run (not agent-reported).

target.title: improve(imessage): manage imsg setup and plugin skill ownership
target.body:
Related: openclaw/imsg#157

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where OpenClaw's bundled iMessage guidance and setup flow lagged the current `imsg` CLI: the OpenClaw copy of the `imsg` skill still lived outside the iMessage plugin, did not document the landed poll behavior, and setup only reported that `imsg` was missing without offering the Homebrew install/update path most local Mac users need.

This is AI-assisted work.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `imsg` skill now lives with the bundled iMessage plugin, matching the existing Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, and QQBot channel-plugin pattern. The old top-level `skills/imsg` copy was removed.

The iMessage setup flow borrows the Signal-style prepare hook to offer macOS Homebrew install/update for the default local `imsg` path, while preserving explicit custom `cliPath` values, including SSH/PATH wrappers. Probe and setup status messages now distinguish default/Homebrew-managed `imsg` from operator-owned wrappers, and doctor can repair stale session snapshot paths to the generated plugin-skill path when that path has been published.

Clanker checked the prior Vincent/Jason history: Vincent previously moved bundled skills into plugin directories with manifest `skills` entries and did not add extra doctor migration. This PR keeps that ownership move, with a conservative doctor repair only for stale session metadata when the generated plugin-skill target exists.

Codex review note: local Codex review repeatedly flagged that moving `imsg` into plugin skills means the skill is only published when the iMessage plugin is activated. I am keeping that behavior because Omar explicitly asked to remove the old skill and align with other channel plugins; the PR body calls out the tradeoff for maintainer review.

## User Impact

Users configuring iMessage on the signed-in Messages Mac can install or update `imsg` from setup instead of manually discovering the command. Existing custom wrapper/SSH setups are left untouched, and setup/probe errors point operators at the configured wrapper when that is what is missing.

Agents using the iMessage skill get updated poll guidance, including the landed `imsg poll send` caption behavior and poll history/watch backfill notes.

target.title: feat(cron): event triggers — polled condition-watcher scripts via code mode
target.body:
Closes #101194

## What Problem This Solves

Watching external state ("wake me when CI on PR 123 changes status") currently requires heartbeat- or cron-waking the full agent so the model can poll — every check burns tokens and adds latency even when nothing changed. Cron had no general event-shaped trigger beyond the `on-exit` process watcher.

## Why This Change Was Made

Cron jobs gain an optional `trigger: { script, once? }` on `every`/`cron` schedules: a JavaScript condition script evaluated headlessly in the existing code-mode QuickJS sandbox on each due tick, with the owning agent's tool policy (`tools.call`) and persisted `trigger.state` for change detection. The script returns `{ fire, message?, state? }`; only `fire: true` runs the payload through the normal cron pipeline (wake modes, delivery, run logs, retry/backoff, failure alerts). Poll-over-push keeps per-source core wiring at zero — anything a tool can reach becomes a trigger source — and the contract leaves room for push sources (webhooks/hook bus) to feed the same scripts later.

Key decisions:
- **Headless driver** (`runCodeModeScriptHeadless`): loops exec → settle bridge tool calls → resume to completion in one call; never stores snapshots, never creates a session, bypasses the agent `exec`/`wait` machinery. Zero changes to the QuickJS worker; `trigger.state` injects via the existing namespace-descriptor path (deep-frozen; scripts return new state).
- **Reliability**: fired-run state persists only when the payload run succeeds, so a failed wake re-detects the change and fires again instead of silently losing the event. Quiet ticks reset error counters, keep per-job cron staggering, and write no `cron_run_logs` rows.
- **Safety**: gated by `cron.triggers.enabled` (default off; enabling means agent-authored scripts run unattended with that agent's full tool policy, including `exec` — docs carry a loud warning). Per-eval budgets: 30s wall clock, 5 tool calls, 16KB state, 30s min poll interval (configurable floor), max 3 concurrent evals, before-tool-call hooks still wrap script-initiated calls.
- **Storage**: script/once stored as columns on `cron_jobs` (additive `ensureColumn` migration, no schema version bump); eval counters/state ride the existing `state_json`.
- **Surfaces**: gateway RPC (`cron.add`/`update` + protocol schemas), agent `cron` tool, CLI (`--trigger-script <path|->`, `--trigger-once`, `--clear-trigger`, list/get display), `triggerFired` on run-log entries. Force-runs bypass evaluation; `once` disarms after the first successful fired payload.

## User Impact

Agents and operators can set up zero-token watchers: "check CI every 30s, wake me only on change." Existing cron jobs and configs are unaffected; the feature is off by default and trigger-bearing jobs validate against the enabled gate at create/patch time. Docs: `docs/automation/cron-jobs.md` gains an "Event triggers (condition watchers)" section.

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

target.title: add per-conversation whatsapp debounce config
target.body:
## Summary

Adds per-conversation inbound debounce configuration for WhatsApp direct chats and groups.

Practically, this controls how long OpenClaw waits before starting an agent turn after receiving a WhatsApp message from a specific conversation. This is useful when a contact sends multiple messages in a row: OpenClaw can wait a few seconds or minutes, collect the full burst, and then let the agent process the conversation with better context.

## What Problem This Solves

The existing WhatsApp debounce setting is too broad for mixed usage.

Some conversations should be processed immediately, while others should wait briefly:

- owner/admin chats often need immediate processing, so they can use `debounceMs: 0`
- external contacts often send multiple short messages in a row, so they can use a longer debounce, such as `180000`, to wait 3 minutes
- noisy groups can have their own debounce window
- wildcard entries can define defaults for all direct chats or all groups

This lets operators tune batching by conversation without changing the global WhatsApp debounce for every chat.

## Behavior

- supports `debounceMs` in `channels.whatsapp.direct`
- supports `debounceMs` in `channels.whatsapp.groups`
- supports wildcard entries like `direct["*"]` and `groups["*"]`
- specific conversation config wins over wildcard config
- falls back to the existing global WhatsApp debounce when no conversation override exists
- `debounceMs: 0` disables debounce for that conversation only

## Evidence

The run used the PR branch plus real WhatsApp session keys from the local OpenClaw session index. The proof output prints only counts and redacted aliases; it does not include phone numbers, group JIDs, contact names, credentials, or message bodies. target.title: fix(heartbeat): skip plugin bootstrap and bundled fallback during delivery target resolution
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a heartbeat wake-loop latency regression where delivery-target resolution blocks for ~60s per tick when the configured channel plugin is not already in the active runtime registry.

### Background

Commit [`6470bb7625`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/6470bb7625) introduced `allowBootstrap: true` in heartbeat delivery-target resolution so plugin channel targets could be loaded on demand. However, `resolveRuntimePluginRegistry()` scans **all** installed plugins — not just the target channel.

### Root cause

`bootstrapAttempts` guard in `channel-bootstrap.runtime.ts`:
- **Success**: key cached → subsequent ticks skip
- **Failure** (plugin not installed / config issue): key deleted → every tick re-scans

## Changes

1. **Hot path**: heartbeat call sites pass `allowBootstrap: false, allowBundledFallback: false`
2. **Startup pre-activation**: `preactivateHeartbeatChannelPlugins()` loads external plugins once before heartbeat loop
3. **Per-agent coverage**: iterates `agents.list[].heartbeat` entries (matching `resolveHeartbeatConfig` merge semantics)
4. **Session-derived `target:last`**: keeps guarded bootstrap (not pre-activatable from config)
5. **Hot reload & override preactivation**: `updateConfig` and `requestHeartbeat` (cron/manual wakes) call preactivation so externally-configured targets introduced after startup are covered
6. **Doctor caller compatibility**: `allowBootstrap` parameter threaded through `resolveHeartbeatDeliveryTarget` so doctor (which runs outside the wake loop) can resolve external plugin targets without preactivation

## Evidence

## Revision (2026-07-06)

Addressed ClawSweeper review findings:

- **P1 — reload gap**: `updateConfig()` in heartbeat runner now calls `preactivateHeartbeatChannelPlugins` before rebuilding the agent schedule
- **P1 — override gap**: `requestHeartbeat()` wake handler pre-activates requested-heartbeat override targets before the no-bootstrap resolver runs

## Revision (2026-07-07) #1

Removed duplicate heartbeat plugin preactivation path identified by ClawSweeper review:

- **P2 — duplicate startup preactivation**: Removed `preactivateHeartbeatChannelPlugins` from `activateGatewayScheduledServices`. The `startHeartbeatRunner` constructor already calls `updateConfig(state.cfg)` which handles the initial preactivation plus all hot-reload/config-update paths. Removing the gateway-side call eliminates a repeated registry scan when an external target fails to load.
- Updated comment in `heartbeat-runner.ts` `updateConfig` to reflect it is now the single preactivation path.
- 147 related tests pass (`server-runtime-services.test.ts`, `heartbeat-runner.scheduler.test.ts`, `heartbeat-pre-activate.test.ts`, `targets.test.ts`).

## Revision (2026-07-07) #2 (a0ba292)

Addressed ClawSweeper [P2] finding — gating preactivation to enabled, deliverable heartbeat configs:

**Problem**: `preactivateHeartbeatChannelPlugins` was called from `updateConfig` before the interval filter (`resolveHeartbeatIntervalMs`). A disabled heartbeat config (`every: "0m"`) with an external target still triggered `resolveOutboundChannelPlugin({ allowBootstrap: true })` during startup/reload, scanning all installed plugins unnecessarily. External targets without a recipient (`to`) were also preactivated even though the runner can never deliver to them.

**Fix in `heartbeat-pre-activate.ts`**:
- Config-scan path (startup/reload): each target is only preactivated when the heartbeat is enabled (`resolveHeartbeatIntervalMs` returns non-null) AND has a deliverable recipient (`to` is set). This mirrors the `updateConfig` scheduling loop which skips agents with `intervalMs === 0`.
- Direct heartbeat override path (cron/manual wakes via `requestHeartbeat`): still preactivates without an interval check because the caller already validated the wake is active. Only skips targets without a recipient.

**New regression tests** (+7 in `heartbeat-pre-activate.test.ts`):
- ✅ Disabled default (`every: "0m"`) → no preactivation
- ✅ Disabled per-agent (`every: "0m"`) → no preactivation
- ✅ Missing `to` on default target → no preactivation
- ✅ Missing `to` on per-agent target → no preactivation
- ✅ Missing `to` on heartbeat override → no preactivation
- ✅ Per-agent with its own `every: "15m"` overrides disabled default → preactivated

**Test results**: 19/19 `heartbeat-pre-activate.test.ts`, 87/87 `targets.test.ts`, 25/25 `heartbeat-runner.scheduler.test.ts` — all pass.

## Revision (2026-07-07) #3 (1334dd29)

Addressed ClawSweeper [P2] finding — skip default target preactivation when explicit per-agent heartbeats override scheduling:

**Problem**: `preactivateHeartbeatChannelPlugins` unconditionally added `agents.defaults.heartbeat` to the target set even when `agents.list[]` entries had their own heartbeat configs. In that case `resolveHeartbeatAgents` schedules only the merged per-agent entries — it does not schedule the default as a standalone target. Preactivating the unused default target caused an unnecessary full-plugin-registry scan on startup/reload.

**Fix in `heartbeat-pre-activate.ts`**:
- Added a `hasExplicitAgents` check mirroring `resolveHeartbeatAgents`: when any `agents.list[]` entry has a `heartbeat` block, the standalone default target is skipped. Only the per-agent effective targets (which may merge `target` or `to` from defaults) are preactivated.
- When no agent has an explicit heartbeat, the default target is still preactivated as before (it is what the scheduler runs).

**Updated tests** (+1 new regression, 2 existing tests adjusted):
- ✅ New: "skips the default external target when a per-agent heartbeat overrides it" — default `unused-external-plugin` with `to: room:default` is not preactivated because agent `override-agent` has its own `background-channel` target
- ✅ Adjusted: "pre-activates distinct external targets from defaults and per-agent configs" → now expects only the per-agent target (default skipped)
- ✅ Adjusted: "pre-activates a per-agent external target that inherits to from defaults" → now expects only the per-agent target with inherited `to` (default skipped)

**Test results**: 21/21 `heartbeat-pre-activate.test.ts`, 87/87 `targets.test.ts`, 25/25 `heartbeat-runner.scheduler.test.ts` — all pass (133 total).

## Revision (2026-07-07) #4 — fix external-target detector (9db74edf)

Addressed ClawSweeper [P1] finding — `isExternalPluginTarget` used wrong helper semantics:

**Problem**: `isExternalPluginTarget` used `normalizeDeliverableOutboundChannel()` and inverted its return value to decide "external plugin." But `normalizeDeliverableOutboundChannel` preserves unknown plugin ids as deliverable (for external-plugin routing), so an explicit external target like `external-channel` made the helper return a truthy value and `isExternalPluginTarget` returned `false` — silently skipping bootstrap preactivation for external plugin targets.

**Root cause in the contract**:
- `normalizeMessageChannel` (in `message-channel-core.ts:27`) preserves unknown-but-normalized ids: `return normalizeAnyChannelId(normalized) ?? normalized`
- `normalizeDeliverableOutboundChannel` wraps `normalizeMessageChannel` + `isDeliverableMessageChannel`, so it returns a truthy value for unknown external plugin channels
- The old `isExternalPluginTarget` inverted this: `return !normalized` — wrong, because the helper returned a value for external channels

**Fix in `heartbeat-pre-activate.ts`**:
- Replaced `normalizeDeliverableOutboundChannel` with `isDeliverableMessageChannel` + `normalizeChatChannelId`
- `isDeliverableMessageChannel(rawTarget)` confirms the target is a deliverable channel id (non-internal, non-empty)
- `!normalizeChatChannelId(rawTarget)` confirms it's NOT a built-in chat channel — built-in channels are already in the bundled catalog and don't need bootstrap
- Only targets that pass both checks (deliverable but not built-in) are classified as external plugin targets

**Updated tests** — `heartbeat-pre-activate.test.ts`:
- Replaced `normalizeDeliverableOutboundChannel` mock with `isDeliverableMessageChannel` + `normalizeChatChannelId` mocks
- `isDeliverableMessageChannel` now returns `true` for any non-empty string (matching real contract: unknown plugin ids are deliverable)
- `normalizeChatChannelId` only returns non-null for built-in channel ids (`telegram`, `discord`, `whatsapp`)
- This means external plugin targets (e.g. `external-channel`) correctly pass `isExternalPluginTarget` — deliverable but not built-in → needs preactivation
- Built-in channel targets (e.g. `telegram`) correctly fail `isExternalPluginTarget` — deliverable AND built-in → skip preactivation

**Test results**: 22/22 `heartbeat-pre-activate.test.ts`, 87/87 `targets.test.ts`, 27/27 `heartbeat-runner.scheduler.test.ts` — all pass (136 total).



## Revision (2026-07-08)

Addressed ClawSweeper [P1] finding — explicit normalized heartbeat plugin targets not honoring caller `allowBootstrap`:

**Problem**: When `normalizeDeliverableOutboundChannel` preserves an external plugin channel id (production normalization contract at `message-channel-core.ts:27-29`), the explicit target reaches the later plugin lookup at `targets.ts:217-225`. That lookup hardcoded `allowBootstrap: isSessionDerived` (always `false` for explicit targets) and `allowBundledFallback: !isSessionDerived` (always `true` for explicit targets). This meant:
- Doctor's `allowBootstrap: true` was ignored → false "replies are dropped silently" warnings for external plugin heartbeat targets
- Bundled fallback was enabled on the heartbeat hot path → could lazy-load bundled channel module code contrary to the performance boundary

**Fix in `targets.ts`**:
- `resolveHeartbeatDeliveryTarget`: plugin lookup now honors `params.allowBootstrap` for explicit targets (`isSessionDerived || params.allowBootstrap === true`) and disables bundled fallback unconditionally (`allowBundledFallback: false`)
- `resolveHeartbeatDeliveryTargetWithSessionRoute`: bundled fallback also disabled in sync with the primary resolution path

**New regression tests** (+2 in `targets.test.ts`):
- ✅ Doctor `allowBootstrap: true` passes through for explicit external targets preserved by production normalization
- ✅ Hot path keeps `allowBootstrap: false` with bundled fallback disabled
- Both tests override the normalization mock to simulate production behavior where external plugin ids are preserved (rather than returning `undefined`)

target.title: fix(agents): avoid false unscheduled note after shell cron add
target.body:
Closes #52972

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users who schedule reminders through a shell-driven `openclaw cron add ...` command could still receive the false note saying no reminder was scheduled in the turn.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reminder guard already trusts successful structured `cron` tool adds. This extends the same producer-side counter to successful `exec` and `bash` commands that run `openclaw cron add` and return a cron add response shaped like the CLI output.

The repair also handles the CLI warning path where `openclaw cron add --message ...` emits the missing-agent warning on stderr while still printing the successful JSON receipt on stdout. Exec aggregates stdout and stderr, so the parser now scans the aggregate for a valid cron-add JSON receipt instead of requiring the whole aggregate to be pure JSON. Failed commands and unrelated cron commands are ignored.

## User Impact

Users no longer get a contradictory unscheduled-reminder note after a shell cron add succeeds, including the default-agent warning case. Failed or unrelated shell commands still leave the guard active.

## Evidence

target.title: test(media): cover filename control-character and bidi/zero-width sanitization
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`sanitizeFilename()` in `src/media/store.ts` is the boundary that turns an
untrusted, caller-supplied media filename into the on-disk name used under the
media store. It strips ASCII control characters (via `sanitizeUntrustedFileName`)
and replaces any run of non-`[\p{L}\p{N}._-]` characters with an underscore.
This matters for security: it neutralizes CR/LF and other control bytes (log/path
injection) and Unicode bidi-override characters used in extension-spoofing
(`report<U+202E>fdp.exe` renders as `reportexe.pdf`).

The existing test coverage for this seam only exercises visible punctuation
(`<`, `>`, `:`, space). The control-character, bidi-override, and zero-width
behaviors were **unverified** — a future simplification of the sanitizer regex
could silently reopen a spoofing or injection hole with no failing test.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add focused regression-lock tests so the security-relevant sanitization behavior
is pinned. This is **test-only**: it asserts the current, already-correct
behavior of `sanitizeFilename` — no production code changes.

## User Impact

None at runtime. This strengthens the safety net around media filename handling
so the sanitizer's security properties cannot regress unnoticed.

## Evidence

Five cases added to the existing `it.each` block in `src/media/store.test.ts`:

- CR/LF stripped: `evil\r\nname.txt` → `evilname---<uuid>.txt`
- C0 controls (tab/FF/ESC/NUL) stripped: `weird\t\f\x1b\x00name.txt` → `weirdname---<uuid>.txt`
- DEL (0x7f) stripped: `deletes\x7fme.txt` → `deletesme---<uuid>.txt`
- Bidi override (U+202E RLO) neutralized to `_`: `report<RLO>fdp.exe` → `report_fdp---<uuid>.txt`
  (stored extension is driven by the buffer/header MIME, not the spoofed suffix)
- Zero-width space + BOM neutralized to `_`: `ze<U+200B>ro<U+FEFF>width.txt` → `ze_ro_width---<uuid>.txt`

Test run against current `main`: `5 passed | 47 skipped`, exit 0
(`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/media/store.test.ts -t "original filename"`).

**Real-behavior proof** — driving the production `saveMediaBuffer` path directly
(no mocks; real MIME detection + real file write to a scratch `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`,
private path redacted), `node --import tsx`:

```
=== real saveMediaBuffer('text/plain') — production path, no mocks ===
CR/LF                  input="evil\r\nname.txt"   -> saved.id = evilname---<uuid>.txt
C0 (tab/FF/ESC/NUL)    input="weird\t\f\x1b\x00name.txt" -> saved.id = weirdname---<uuid>.txt
DEL 0x7f               input="deletes\x7fme.txt"  -> saved.id = deletesme---<uuid>.txt
U+202E RLO spoof       input="report<RLO>fdp.exe" -> saved.id = report_fdp---<uuid>.txt
zero-width + BOM       input="ze<ZWSP>ro<BOM>width.txt" -> saved.id = ze_ro_width---<uuid>.txt
```

Security observation from the RLO case: the on-disk name is `report_fdp---<uuid>.txt` —
the spoofed `.exe` suffix never reaches disk (stored extension is MIME-driven `.txt`,
and the bidi override is replaced by `_`).

target.title: fix(agents): add lock release timeout on attempt teardown
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an agent run fails abnormally during tool execution (e.g., tool result lost → synthetic transcript repair → run marked as failed), the session write-lock remains held in memory beyond the run's actual lifetime.

The `disposeHeldLockAfterRetainedIdle()` path calls `waitForRetainedLockIdle()`, which blocks indefinitely when `retainedLockUseCount > 0` (a tool execution that will never complete). The `finally` block in `attempt.ts` hangs at `releaseRetainedSessionLock()`, so the lock is never released. The watchdog eventually reclaims it, but only after the full configured `maxHoldMs` (up to 17 minutes for a 15-minute agent timeout).

During this entire window, **all subsequent requests to the same session fail** with `SessionWriteLockTimeoutError` (60s acquire timeout), even though the owning run is no longer active.

### Observed behavior

```
session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=72859
```

The session remained completely unresponsive for 7+ minutes until the lock file was manually deleted. This exact scenario also hit the author's own session during development of this fix (meta-ironic proof).

## Why This Change Was Made

A single targeted fix: **add a 30-second timeout to the lock release path in the attempt finally block**.

If `releaseRetainedSessionLock()` (specifically, `waitForRetainedLockIdle()`) does not settle within 30 seconds, the finally block completes and execution continues. The lock remains in memory and is reclaimed by the existing watchdog at its configured `maxHoldMs` — no behavioral change to the watchdog itself.

Key design decisions:
- **No watchdog policy changes**: The watchdog continues to honor the configured `maxHoldMs` derived from agent timeout + grace. Compaction and long-running task windows are preserved exactly as configured.
- **Timer hygiene**: The timeout is extracted into a focused helper (`attempt.release-lock-timeout.ts`) that uses `.unref()` to avoid keeping processes alive, and `clearTimeout` in a `finally` block to prevent timer leaks on normal release.
- **Minimal blast radius**: Only the attempt teardown path is affected. Normal runs that release promptly never see the timeout.

## User Impact

Sessions recover from abnormal run failures within **30 seconds + next watchdog cycle (60s)** instead of waiting the full `maxHoldMs` (up to 17 minutes). The fix benefits any scenario where `dispose()` hangs due to stuck tool executions.

## Evidence

**Root cause trace (from real production incident):**
1. Agent run executing `exec` tool → command not found → tool result lost
2. Synthetic error result injected for transcript repair
3. Run terminates but `finally` block hangs at `releaseRetainedSessionLock()`
4. Lock still in `SESSION_LOCKS.heldEntries()` → `heldByThisProcess = true` → orphan-self-pid skipped
5. Watchdog threshold = 17 minutes → session blocked for entire duration

**Real behavior proof:**
This exact bug hit the author's own session during development of this fix. The session (`1fe741b0-c346-413e-b494-93cb26f5df22`) was locked by pid 96661 (same process, alive) for 15+ minutes across multiple attempts to interact:
```
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=435021
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=679231
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=753583
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=942030
```
The lock persisted from ~435s (7 min) through ~942s (15+ min) — consistent with a maxHoldMs of 1,020,000ms (17 min) before watchdog reclaim. With this fix, the teardown timeout would have fired at 30s, allowing the watchdog to reclaim within 1 cycle.

**Test results:**
- `attempt.release-lock-timeout.test.ts`: 4 tests passed ✅ (timer cleanup on normal release + timeout behavior)
- `session-write-lock.test.ts`: 106 tests passed ✅ (no regression to watchdog logic)
- oxlint: 0 warnings, 0 errors ✅

Fixes #100872

target.title: feat(session-message-events) socket.drain
target.body:
## Summary

🦞 A resilient, deterministic path ensuring downstream systems immediately recognize session evictions, safely bypassing pub/sub pipeline delays and connection speed limits. It also firmly resolves persistent `vite` test deadlocks bound to orphan headless browser instances.
- **Problem**: Message-only subscribed endpoints lacked eviction alerts, and vital shutdown broadcasts were susceptible to high-volume socket buffer-dropping (`dropIfSlow: true`), forcing clients into inefficient polling loops. Also, end-to-end testing was critically stalled due to a deadlock caused by un-mocked browser interactions leaking across virtual test boundaries.
- **Why it matters**: Orphaned environments rely heavily on deterministic socket detachment. Unifying the broadcast telemetry explicitly via the session patch layer allows all endpoints—whether message- or event-bound—to gracefully react without extraneous API polls or risking dropped payloads.
- **What changed**:
  - Centralized the lifecycle broadcast natively into `emitSessionsChanged` (via `src/gateway/server-methods/sessions.ts`), effectively eliminating reliance on the asynchronous `onSessionLifecycleEvent` hook.
  - Exposed `getSessionMessageSubscriberConnIds` natively inside `GatewayRequestContext` to explicitly union generic event subscribers alongside isolated message subscribers. 
  - Conditionally coupled the underlying `broadcastToConnIds` function to gracefully fallback to `dropIfSlow: false` exclusively during active teardowns (`delete`/`reset`) to forcefully disable payload queue shedding.
  - Registered `"socket.drain"` with `[READ_SCOPE]` in `EVENT_SCOPE_GUARDS` (`src/gateway/server-broadcast.ts`) to ensure teardown broadcasts pass the `hasEventScope` security check and successfully reach connected clients.
  - Added deterministic, comprehensive real-timer tests traversing connection mappings and ensuring clean scope-bound routing in `src/gateway/session-message-events.test.ts`.
  - Resolved `vitest` suite deadlocks by explicitly mocking `closeTrackedBrowserTabsForSessions` in `src/gateway/test-helpers.mocks.ts` to prevent HTTP request leaks against dead CDP instances.
- **What did NOT change (scope boundary)**: No existing contracts or `socket.drain` payloads were modified in structure. This is 100% additive logic expanding target scope precision.
